title: Uthman, the modest
hookLine: gentle and generous, called the possessor of two lights for marrying two of the Prophet's daughters

lines: A KNOCK, AND HE SITS UP.
cards: Aisha tells it, in Sahih Muslim. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is lying down at home, relaxed, his garment pulled up a little from his leg. A knock.
Abu Bakr asks to come in. He's welcomed, the Prophet stays just as he is, and they talk. Another knock: Umar.
Same thing. He comes in, they talk, nothing changes. A third knock, and this time the Prophet sits up and straightens his clothes before the visitor enters.
Aisha notices, and afterward she asks him why. The visitor was Uthman.

teach.h: SHALL I NOT BE SHY BEFORE HIM?
teach.b: His answer to Aisha, in the report: shall I not be shy before a man the angels are shy before? The word behind that is haya'.

In English it gets translated as modesty, shyness, or bashfulness, but none of those quite fits. Haya' is a kind of inner tact: a sense of what is fitting before God and before people, and a reluctance to cross that line.

In a hadith in Bukhari, the Prophet says that haya' is a branch of faith, and in another, that haya' brings nothing but good. So when he straightens his clothes for Uthman, he is meeting a modest man with modesty.
Uthman ibn Affan was a wealthy merchant from Mecca, remembered as a gentle one.
Tradition gives him a second name: Dhu al-Nurayn, the one with two lights. The usual explanation is that he married two of the Prophet's daughters, Ruqayyah, and after her death, Umm Kulthum.
He was generous, too, and his generosity had the same quiet shape. On another day this path saw him equip an army. Tomorrow, a well.

Later he became the third caliph, honored by Sunni Muslims among the rightly guided caliphs, while Shia Muslims view the succession differently. But the scene this tradition keeps is small. Not a battle, not a speech.
A man so modest that even the Prophet sat up when he knocked.

how: Muslims speak of haya', modesty and inner tact, as part of faith, and often hold up Uthman ibn Affan as its example; Sunni Muslims honor him as the third caliph.

o: the companion who carried the flag at Khaybar
the companion who first called the prayer
the gentle companion known for his modesty

games.q: uthman, the modest — tap the pairs.
p: he sat up and straightened his clothes

s: the Prophet sat up for Abu Bakr and Umar too
he stayed as he was for them, and sat up only when Uthman came in.
a hadith calls haya' a branch of faith
Dhu al-Nurayn refers to his two lamps at home
tradition explains the two lights as his marriages to two of the Prophet's daughters.

games.q: you're Aisha. Abu Bakr and Umar came in and nothing changed. then Uthman knocks, and the Prophet sits up and straightens his clothes. what do you do?
o: say nothing; it's not your business.
games.why: she asked, and he said: shall I not be shy before a man the angels are shy before?

practice: Think of something you could give that nobody needs to know came from you: a paid bill, a bag of groceries left at a door, a kind word passed to someone's boss, a donation with no name on it.
Notice whether there's any pull to be seen giving it, and if there is, let it soften. If you pray, ask Allah to accept it, and keep it between the two of you.

wordCard.voice: Uthman. Uthman ibn Affan, the gentle, generous companion called Dhu al-Nurayn, the one with two lights, and known for haya', modesty. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: modesty, shyness, an inner sense of what is fitting.

carryVoice: Your line: the modest one. Haya', answered by haya', at the third knock. That's day eight hundred three.
